x: Under Article 79, Parliament consists of the President, the Lok Sabha and the Rajya Sabha. The President is part of Parliament but not a member of either House.
t: Discriminate between being part of Parliament and being a member of a House.

x: An ordinary bill can be introduced in either House. Only Money Bills and Financial Bills under Article 117(1) must start in the Lok Sabha.
t: Recall which bills must start in the Lok Sabha.

x: Option C is incorrect: there is no joint sitting on a Money Bill, because the Rajya Sabha can only recommend within 14 days and the Lok Sabha decides. A Money Bill starts in the Lok Sabha on the President's recommendation.
t: Recall the two kinds of bill excluded from joint sittings.

x: Both are true: a Financial Bill under Article 117(1) starts only in the Lok Sabha, on the President's recommendation. One under Article 117(3) can start in either House, but needs the recommendation before it is considered.
t: Discriminate recommendation for introduction (117(1)) from recommendation for consideration (117(3)).

x: I, II and III are correct: on dissolution, bills pending in the Lok Sabha, or passed by it and pending in the Rajya Sabha, lapse, but a bill pending in the Rajya Sabha that the Lok Sabha never passed survives. IV is false because prorogation ends no bill.
t: Trace which House each bill is pending in when the Lok Sabha dissolves.

x: Ordinary bills come under Articles 107–108, Money Bills under 109–110, Financial Bills (I) under 117(1), and amendment bills under 368. The answer is a-i, b-ii, c-iii, d-iv.
t: Recall the Article for each kind of bill.

x: Article 108 covers the joint sitting, 111 the President's assent, 116 the vote on account, and 200 the Governor's action on State bills. The answer is a-ii, b-i, c-iii, d-iv.
t: Recall each Article's subject.

x: The general discussion on a bill's principles happens at the second reading. The first reading is introduction and the third is passing.
t: Recall what happens at each of the three readings.

x: Option B is incorrect: a Legislative Council can delay an ordinary bill for at most four months (three, then one), not six. A State Money Bill starts in the Assembly on the Governor's recommendation, and the Council has 14 days to consider it.
t: Recall the Council's 3 + 1 month limit.

x: Both are true: the President summons a joint sitting and the Lok Sabha Speaker presides over it. Who summons it does not explain who presides, so R does not explain A.
t: Ask whether who summons explains who presides.

x: Three are correct: an amendment bill can start in either House without the President's recommendation, and needs a special majority in each House separately. Statement 3 is false because there is no joint sitting for it.
t: Recall that amendment bills have no joint sitting.

x: A Private Member's Bill is introduced by any MP who is not a Minister, whether elected or nominated. A Minister's bill is a Government Bill.
t: Discriminate between Private Member's and Government Bills.

x: Both are true: a bill is proposed law, and it becomes an Act only with the President's assent under Article 111. That later step does not explain what a bill is, so R does not explain A.
t: Ask whether a later step can define what a bill is.

x: All four are correct: an ordinary bill needs a simple majority, both Houses have equal powers over it, a deadlock can go to a joint sitting, and the Rajya Sabha has no fixed time limit on it.
t: Contrast ordinary bills with the 14-day limit on Money Bills.

x: Three are correct: a Money Bill starts only in the Lok Sabha on the President's recommendation and covers taxes, borrowing and the Consolidated Fund. Statement 4 is false because a bill only about fines or penalties is not a Money Bill (Article 110(2)).
t: Recall the Article 110(2) exclusions.

x: Under Article 110(3), the Lok Sabha Speaker's decision on whether a bill is a Money Bill is final. Neither the President nor the Rajya Sabha Chairman can overrule it.
t: Recall who certifies Money Bills.

x: A Financial Bill (I) contains Article 110 matters plus general law. The Rajya Sabha can reject or amend it, and a deadlock can go to a joint sitting. The answer is a-i, b-ii, c-iii, d-iv.
t: Discriminate Financial Bill (I) from Money Bills.

x: All three are correct: a Financial Bill (II) involves spending from the Consolidated Fund but contains no Article 110 matter. It is treated as an ordinary bill, so a joint sitting is possible.
t: Remember that Financial Bill (II) follows ordinary-bill procedure.

x: All four are correct: an amendment bill cannot start in a State Legislature, needs a special majority (majority of total membership plus two-thirds present and voting), and federal changes need half the States. The President must give assent.
t: Recall each step of the Article 368 procedure.

x: Both are true: since the 24th Amendment, the President must assent to an amendment bill, which leaves no room for a veto. R explains A.
t: Ask whether compulsory assent explains the lack of a veto.

x: Three are correct: an ordinary bill needs no prior recommendation and passes by simple majority, and a Money Bill also passes by simple majority. Statement 4 is false because a Money Bill does not need a special majority.
t: Recall which bills need a special majority.

x: All six are correct: the President can assent to, withhold or return once an ordinary bill. A Money Bill can be assented to or withheld but never returned.
t: Discriminate the President's options on ordinary bills and Money Bills.

x: All six are correct: a joint sitting is for ordinary bills, called by the President, presided over by the Speaker (then the Deputy Speaker, then the Deputy Chairman), and has a quorum of one-tenth. It decides by simple majority.
t: Check the order of who presides and the quorum.

x: If the President has already notified a joint sitting, the bill does not lapse when the Lok Sabha dissolves. The joint sitting can still be held.
t: Recall the exception to bills lapsing on dissolution.

x: Both are true: State Money Bills come under Articles 198, 199 and 207. The Governor can reserve a State bill for the President under Article 200, and the President deals with it under Article 201.
t: Recall the State-level Articles 198–201.

x: Both are true: every Money Bill is a Financial Bill, but not every Financial Bill is a Money Bill. The second fact is the converse, not the reason for the first, so R does not explain A.
t: Ask whether a converse statement can explain the original.

x: Three joint sittings have been held: the Dowry Prohibition Bill (1961), the Banking Service Commission Repeal Bill (1978) and POTA (2002).
t: Recall the three joint sittings.

x: The Dowry Prohibition Bill went to a joint sitting in 1961, the Banking Service Commission Repeal Bill in 1978 and POTA in 2002. The answer is a-ii, b-iii, c-i.
t: Recall the order of the three joint sittings.

x: Both are true: Giani Zail Singh used a pocket veto on the Indian Post Office (Amendment) Bill, 1986, and Rajendra Prasad used an absolute veto on the PEPSU Appropriation Bill, 1954.
t: Recall each President's use of the veto.

x: Articles 109–110 cover Money Bills, 112 the Budget, 113 demands for grants, 114 the Appropriation Bill, 117 Financial Bills and 368 amendments. The answer is a-iv, b-i, c-v, d-vi, e-ii, f-iii.
t: Remember that Articles 112 to 114 run in budget order: statement, demands, appropriation.

x: An ordinary bill can start in either House, with equal powers. A Money Bill starts in the Lok Sabha and the Rajya Sabha can only recommend. An amendment bill can start in either House and must pass each separately. A Financial Bill (I) starts in the Lok Sabha but can be rejected or amended. The answer is a-i, b-ii, c-iii, d-iv.
t: Compare where each bill starts and the Rajya Sabha's power over it.

x: All three are correct: a joint sitting under Article 108 can settle a deadlock on an ordinary bill, but not on a Money Bill or an amendment bill.
t: Recall the two kinds of bill excluded from joint sittings.

x: Both are true: an amendment bill must pass each House separately by special majority, and it can start in either House without a recommendation. Where it starts does not explain the separate passage, so R does not explain A.
t: Ask whether where a bill starts explains how it passes.

x: The Rajya Sabha can only make recommendations on a Money Bill, within 14 days. It cannot amend or reject it, and the Lok Sabha may ignore the recommendations.
t: Recall the Rajya Sabha's recommendatory role.

x: A no-confidence motion comes under Rule 198 of the Lok Sabha Rules, not the Constitution. Rule 184 is for a discussion with a vote, 377 for special mentions and 8(1) for the Deputy Speaker's election.
t: Discriminate Rules 198, 184, 377 and 8(1).

x: Option C is incorrect: leave to move a no-confidence motion needs at least 50 members, not 30. It is moved only in the Lok Sabha, against the whole Council of Ministers, with written notice to the Secretary-General.
t: Recall the 50-member requirement.

x: Both are true: Zero Hour is not in the Constitution because it is an informal convention, found in neither the Constitution nor the Rules. R explains A.
t: Ask whether informal origin explains absence from the Constitution.

x: A is true: a starred question gets an oral answer, with supplementaries. B is false because an unstarred question gets a written answer and allows no supplementaries.
t: Check whether each kind of question allows supplementaries.

x: Rule 198 is the no-confidence motion, 184 a discussion with a vote, 377 special mentions, and 8(1) the Deputy Speaker's election. The answer is a-ii, b-iv, c-iii, d-i.
t: Recall each Lok Sabha rule's subject.

x: I, II and IV are correct: Question Hour is the first hour, Zero Hour follows it, and Zero Hour is for urgent matters. III is false because Question Hour is formal and in the Rules; Zero Hour is the informal one.
t: Discriminate formal Question Hour from informal Zero Hour.

x: Two kinds allow supplementaries, starred and short notice questions, because both are answered orally. Unstarred questions get written answers and none.
t: Remember that only oral-answer questions allow supplementaries.

x: In 2015, the daily limit of matters under Rule 377 was raised from 20 to 30.
t: Recall the 2015 change to Rule 377.

x: Both are true: an adjournment motion implies censure, and it interrupts business for an urgent, recent matter. R describes the procedure, not the reason for the censure, so R does not explain A.
t: Ask whether a procedure explains a censure element.

x: Both are true: Article 110 defines Money Bills and Article 108 provides for joint sittings.
t: Recall Articles 108 and 110.

x: The Constitution sets only the broad framework for Lok Sabha proceedings. The day-to-day procedure is in the Rules of Procedure and Conduct of Business in Lok Sabha.
t: Discriminate the Constitution's framework from the House's Rules.

x: Both are true: Rule 377 is not in the Constitution because it comes from the House's own Rules of Procedure. R explains A.
t: Ask whether the rule's source explains its absence from the Constitution.

x: All three are correct: Question Hour, supplementary questions and adjournment motions are the main tools of executive accountability, the 'accountability triangle'.
t: Recall the three parts of the accountability triangle.

x: Both are true: the government moves a confidence motion and it shows the majority on the floor. Who moves it does not explain what it shows, so R does not explain A.
t: Ask whether who moves a motion explains its effect.

x: Both are true: Rule 184 allows a discussion that ends in a vote, so losing that vote has serious political consequences for the government.
t: Recall that Rule 184 involves a vote.

x: All three are correct: Rule 377 is for matters that cannot be raised through questions, calling attention or other motions, and it needs written notice and the Speaker's consent.
t: Recall the conditions of Rule 377.

x: Both are true: under Rule 8(1), the Speaker fixes the date of the Deputy Speaker's election and the Secretary-General notifies it to members.
t: Discriminate who fixes the date from who notifies it.

x: All four are correct: Question Hour runs from 11 AM to noon and Zero Hour from noon to 1 PM. Zero Hour is an Indian innovation from the early 1960s.
t: Recall the timings and origin of Zero Hour.

x: All three are correct: Question Hour is for asking and answering the three kinds of questions and lasts one hour, and Zero Hour usually lasts up to an hour.
t: Check each duration.

x: At most 20 starred questions are listed each day for oral answer. Unstarred questions have no such limit.
t: Recall the daily limit of 20 starred questions.

x: All three are correct: a short notice question concerns an urgent public matter, is asked with less than 10 clear days' notice, and gets an oral answer.
t: Recall the notice period and kind of answer.

x: Both are true: the calling attention motion is an Indian innovation for urgent matters, and it resembles an adjournment motion without the censure. That difference does not explain why it is Indian, so R does not explain A.
t: Ask whether lacking censure explains being an Indian innovation.

x: All four are correct: closure cuts debate short and puts the question to vote, and the guillotine is the form used when the allotted time runs out, putting all remaining clauses or demands to vote at once.
t: Discriminate closure in general from the guillotine.

x: Under Article 85, the President summons each House, and no more than six months may pass between sessions. Article 123 is about ordinances.
t: Recall Article 85's six-month rule.

x: Option B is incorrect: prorogation ends the session, not the House. Only dissolution ends the House, and only the Lok Sabha can be dissolved.
t: Rank the four by how much they end: sitting, session, House.

x: Adjournment sine die ends a sitting without naming a date, recess is the gap between sessions, the quorum is the minimum for business, and Zero Hour is for urgent matters without notice. The answer is a-iv, b-ii, c-i, d-iii.
t: Match each term to its definition.

x: I and II are correct: Zero Hour follows Question Hour and is an Indian innovation. III is false because no prior formal notice is needed.
t: Remember that Zero Hour needs no notice.

x: An unstarred question gets a written answer and allows no supplementaries. Starred and short notice questions are answered orally.
t: Discriminate written answers from oral answers.

x: Option C is incorrect: a calling attention motion has no censure element; an adjournment motion does. A no-confidence motion needs 50 members and is only for the Lok Sabha, and a censure motion must state reasons.
t: Discriminate which motions carry censure.

x: Both are true: an adjournment motion sets aside normal business for an urgent matter, and a closure motion ends debate and puts the matter to vote.
t: Recall what each motion does to business.

x: The Annual Financial Statement is the Constitution's name for the Budget, the Appropriation Bill permits withdrawals, a vote on account is an advance grant, and a vote of credit is an emergency grant. The answer is a-ii, b-iv, c-i, d-iii.
t: Discriminate the advance grant (vote on account) from the emergency grant (vote of credit).

x: Three are correct: a policy cut reduces a demand to ₹1, an economy cut by a specified amount, and a token cut by ₹100. Statement 4 is false because charged expenditure is discussed but not voted on.
t: Recall that charged expenditure is not voted on.

x: Habeas corpus ends unlawful detention, mandamus orders a duty to be done, certiorari quashes a lower court's order, and quo warranto challenges a claim to public office. The answer is a-iii, b-ii, c-iv, d-i.
t: Recall each writ's purpose from its Latin name.

x: The Basic Structure Doctrine was laid down in Kesavananda Bharati v. State of Kerala (1973). 1975 is the Indira Gandhi election case, which applied the doctrine.
t: Recall the case and year of the Basic Structure Doctrine.

x: I and II are correct: judicial review is an inherent power of constitutional courts to test laws and executive action. III is false because the basic structure cannot be destroyed even under Article 368.
t: Find the statement that contradicts the Basic Structure Doctrine.

x: A pardon removes both sentence and conviction, commutation swaps a punishment for a lighter one, remission shortens a sentence, and a reprieve postpones execution. The answer is a-ii, b-iv, c-iii, d-i.
t: Discriminate the five kinds of pardon by what each changes.

x: Option C is incorrect: first-past-the-post is a plurality system, so the candidate with the most votes wins without needing over 50%. PR-STV is used for the President, Vice-President, Rajya Sabha and Legislative Councils.
t: Discriminate plurality (FPTP) from absolute majority.

x: Both are true: delimitation redraws constituency boundaries using recent census figures so that each seat has roughly equal population.
t: Recall the basis and aim of delimitation.

x: A is true: under Article 243B, the intermediate tier (Panchayat Samiti) is optional in States with a population of 20 lakh or less. R is false because it denies that exception.
t: Recall the 20-lakh exception for the intermediate tier.

x: Charged expenditure is paid straight from the Consolidated Fund and can be discussed but not voted on. Option C describes a vote on account and B a vote of credit.
t: Recall that charged expenditure is not voted on.

x: All three are correct: the 1919 Act brought dyarchy to the provinces, with reserved subjects under the Governor and Executive Council and transferred subjects under the Governor and elected Ministers.
t: Discriminate reserved from transferred subjects.

x: A session runs from a House's first sitting to its prorogation or dissolution. A sitting is one day's meeting within it.
t: Discriminate session, sitting and recess.

x: By convention, Parliament has three sessions: Budget, Monsoon and Winter. There is no 'Spring Session'.
t: Recall the three conventional sessions.

x: Both are true: a sitting is the House's daily meeting during a session, and it may have morning and post-lunch parts.
t: Discriminate a sitting from a session.

x: Adjournment ends a sitting for a set time, adjournment sine die ends it without a date, prorogation ends the session, and dissolution ends the House. The answer is a-iii, b-iv, c-ii, d-i.
t: Rank the four by how much they end: sitting, session, House.

x: The President prorogues the Houses under Article 85(2)(a), and dissolves the Lok Sabha under 85(2)(b).
t: Recall the clauses of Article 85(2).

x: Both are true: a recess is the gap between prorogation and the next session, and during it the President can issue ordinances under Article 123.
t: Recall when the President can issue ordinances.

x: Both are true: a closure motion ends debate and puts the matter to vote, and the guillotine is one kind of closure, used when time runs out. Defining one kind does not explain the general device, so R does not explain A.
t: Ask whether defining one kind explains the general device.

x: A no-confidence motion tests the majority, a confidence motion proves it, a censure motion disapproves of specific policies, and calling attention draws a Minister's notice. The answer is a-iii, b-iv, c-i, d-ii.
t: Discriminate who moves each motion and what it aims at.

x: I, II and III are correct: a no-confidence motion is for the Lok Sabha only, comes under Rule 198 and needs 50 members. IV is false because it needs no reasons; a censure motion does.
t: Discriminate the no-confidence motion from the censure motion.

x: Option C is incorrect: a censure motion is moved against a Minister or the whole Council of Ministers, not the Speaker. It must state reasons and expresses disapproval of specific policies.
t: Recall whom a censure motion can be moved against.

x: A short notice question is about an urgent public matter and gets an oral answer, with supplementaries allowed.
t: Recall the kind of answer each question gets.

x: A vote of credit is an emergency grant, like a blank cheque, for a need whose details cannot be stated in the budget. Option A describes a vote on account.
t: Discriminate the vote of credit from the vote on account.

x: Option A is incorrect: a reprieve only postpones execution. Removing both sentence and conviction is a pardon. Commutation, respite and remission are described correctly.
t: Discriminate a reprieve from a pardon.

x: The right to vote in India is a legal (statutory) right under the Representation of the People Act. It is not a Fundamental Right, though Article 326 provides adult suffrage.
t: Discriminate legal rights from Fundamental Rights.

x: The Annual Financial Statement is Article 112, the Appropriation Bill 114, the vote on account 116, and ordinances during recess 123. The answer is a-iii, b-iv, c-ii, d-i.
t: Recall the Articles 112, 114, 116 and 123.

x: Under Article 100, the quorum is one-tenth of the House's total membership.
t: Recall the quorum fraction.

x: A respite gives a lesser sentence because of special circumstances such as pregnancy or disability. Remission shortens a sentence without changing its nature.
t: Discriminate a respite from remission.

x: Option B is incorrect: swapping a punishment for a lighter one is commutation. Remission shortens a sentence, such as two years' rigorous imprisonment to one, without changing its nature.
t: Discriminate remission from commutation.

x: Certiorari is both curative and preventive: a higher court uses it to quash an order a lower court or tribunal has already passed without jurisdiction or in error of law. Prohibition is only preventive.
t: Discriminate certiorari (after an order) from prohibition (before one).

x: Under the Basic Structure Doctrine, the Constitution's core features cannot be destroyed even by amendment under Article 368.
t: Recall the power the Basic Structure Doctrine limits.

x: Both are true: under Article 75(3), the Council of Ministers answers to the Lok Sabha as one body, which is why all Ministers sink or swim together. R explains A.
t: Ask whether collective answerability explains 'sink or swim together'.

x: All three are correct: the three-tier Panchayati Raj system applies in every State, with one exception: its intermediate tier, the Panchayat Samiti, is optional where the population is 20 lakh or less.
t: Recall the 20-lakh exception for the intermediate tier.

x: A no-confidence motion needs 50 members, the government moves a confidence motion, a censure motion must state reasons, and calling attention carries no censure. The answer is a-iii, b-i, c-ii, d-iv.
t: Match each motion to its distinctive feature.

x: I and II are correct: the Appropriation Bill permits withdrawals from the Consolidated Fund for voted grants and charged expenditure. III is false because an advance grant for part of the year is a vote on account.
t: Discriminate the Appropriation Bill from the vote on account.

x: Three are correct: habeas corpus ends illegal detention, mandamus orders a duty to be done, and quo warranto challenges a claim to office. Statement 3 is false because prohibition prevents an order; quashing one already passed is certiorari.
t: Discriminate prohibition from certiorari.

x: All three are correct: first-past-the-post is a plurality system, so over 50% is not needed. PR-STV uses ranked preferences and a quota in indirect elections.
t: Discriminate FPTP from PR-STV.

x: The President's pardoning power is in Article 72 and the Governor's in Article 161. Articles 74 and 163 deal with ministerial advice.
t: Pair the President's Article (72) with the Governor's (161).

x: Both are true: the presiding officer adjourns the House, and the Speaker or Chairman is that officer. R explains A.
t: Ask whether R names who holds the power in A.

x: Both are true: a policy cut (to ₹1) shows complete disapproval of the policy, and an economy cut demands savings in expenditure.
t: Discriminate the aim of each cut motion.

x: Commutation replaces a punishment with a lighter one, such as a death sentence with rigorous life imprisonment. Remission only shortens the term.
t: Discriminate commutation from remission.
